title: Estimation of Propagated Risk in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026]
Title:Estimation of Propagated Risk in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large Language Model (LLM) based multi-agent systems introduce a distinctive reliability challenge in which actions taken by upstream agents can affect the correctness of downstream agents. While prior work has investigated error propagation and developed methods for estimating uncertainty inherited from upstream agents, existing approaches do not explicitly model how realized sender-receiver interactions contribute to downstream error risk under different sender correctness states. In this work, we study agent-level error-risk estimation from multi-agent execution traces. We propose Interaction-Effect Propagation (IE-Prop), an interaction-conditioned model that learns separate effects for correct and incorrect upstream agents. For each sender-receiver interaction, the model combines these conditional effects using the sender's estimated error risk, and recursively propagates the resulting risk estimates through the execution graph. We evaluate our approach across three multi-agent architectures and three benchmarks. Across all evaluated architectures, our approach raises the final-node AUROC over the established baseline by approximately 0.05 points on average. Furthermore, tracking risk across multiple agent steps contributes a distinct +0.03 AUROC gain in sequential systems. These results show that realized inter-agent interactions provide predictive information beyond receiver-local evidence, while the value of multi-step risk tracking depends on the system's information-flow structure.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper introduces IE-Prop, a model that predicts how errors spread between agents in LLM multi-agent systems, improving final-step risk-detection AUROC by roughly 0.05.
report.background: Multi-agent LLM systems — pipelines, orchestrator-worker setups, critic loops and debate frameworks — chain many model calls, so a single bad step can silently corrupt everything downstream. Practitioners have responded with tracing, guardrails and uncertainty estimates, and prior research has documented that errors do propagate between agents and has tried to quantify inherited uncertainty. But most existing approaches score a step using receiver-local evidence: the agent's own confidence, log-probabilities, or self-consistency. They do not explicitly model what actually passed between agents — the realized message — nor how that interaction's effect differs depending on whether the upstream agent was right or wrong. As agent stacks move from demos into production, where a wrong tool call or hallucinated fact can cascade into real transactions, teams need per-step risk estimates precise enough to trigger a retry, a fallback model, or human escalation.
key_points: IE-Prop learns two separate interaction effects for every sender-receiver edge: one for when the upstream agent is correct and one for when it is wrong. At runtime it blends these conditional effects using the sender's own estimated error risk, then recursively propagates the resulting scores along the execution graph — turning a whole trace into a per-node risk profile.

The central claim is that the realized interaction carries signal a receiver cannot see locally. Two runs where a downstream agent receives correct versus incorrect input can look similar from the receiver's confidence alone, yet imply very different failure odds. Conditioning on the actual message exchange captures this, which receiver-local baselines miss.

Evaluated on three benchmarks across three multi-agent architectures, IE-Prop raised final-node AUROC by about 0.05 over the established baseline on average — a meaningful gain for error-detection tasks, where small AUC differences translate into many caught or missed failures at scale.

Tracking risk across multiple agent steps added a further +0.03 AUROC, but only in sequential systems. In architectures where information flows more diffusely, multi-step tracking added little, suggesting propagation-aware monitoring pays off most in linear pipelines rather than parallel fan-out designs.

Because the method operates on execution traces rather than model weights, it is largely model-agnostic and drop-in for existing agent frameworks — though it still needs labeled or reliably estimated correctness signals for upstream agents in order to train the conditional effects.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this pushes agent reliability from ad-hoc guardrails toward calibrated, graph-aware risk scoring — a prerequisite for letting agents act autonomously in high-stakes workflows. Developers get a concrete design lesson: instrument traces at the interaction level, and remember that monitoring payoffs depend on topology, so sequential pipelines benefit more than parallel ones. Expect orchestration frameworks to add risk as a first-class field on edges, enabling automatic retry, rerouting to stronger models, or human hand-off. For regular users, the visible effect is fewer silent failures — agents that notice a bad upstream step and stop rather than confidently compounding it. Caveat: a 0.05 AUROC gain is incremental, and the method still depends on reliable upstream error estimates and labeled traces.
report.tools: To follow up: trace-level observability tools are the natural home for this kind of risk scoring — LangSmith, Arize Phoenix (OpenTelemetry-based) and Weights & Biases Weave all capture per-step agent spans. For reproducing the setup, LangGraph, AutoGen and CrewAI cover the pipeline, fan-out and debate topologies the paper tests. Related research worth reading includes semantic entropy for uncertainty, conformal prediction for LLMs, and prior error-propagation studies. The paper's arXiv page lists code and data links via alphaXiv, CatalyzeX and Hugging Face.
